query.content: According to the paper titled Open-ended Long Text Generation via Masked Language Modeling, what are the main contributions of this research?

ground_truth.content: The paper makes several key contributions: it is the first to explore Open-ended Long Text Generation (Open-LTG) with Non-Autoregressive (NAR) models based on pre-trained Masked Language Models (MLMs) and identifies their collapse problem for long text generation. To address this, it introduces Dynamic Sliding Window Attention (DSWA) to alleviate long-distance collapse problems and Linear Temperature Decay (LTD) to maintain more informative context content and improve sampling effectiveness in iterative NAR generation. Finally, the research demonstrates that pre-trained MLMs, when enhanced with DSWA and LTD, can achieve a significant speedup of more than $3\times \to 13\times$ with better performance compared to strong autoregressive (AR) models on Open-LTG tasks.
references: Pre-trained autoregressive (AR) language models such as BART and GPTs have dominated Open-ended Long Text Generation (Open-LTG). However, the AR nature will decrease the inference efficiency along with the increase of generation length, which hinder their application in Open-LTG. To improve inference efficiency, we alternatively explore the potential of the pre-trained masked language models (MLMs) along with a representative iterative non-autoregressive (NAR) decoding strategy for Open-LTG. Our preliminary study shows that pre-trained MLMs can merely generate short text and will collapse for long text modeling. To enhance the long text generation capability of MLMs, we introduce two simple yet effective strategies for the iterative NAR model: dynamic sliding window attention (DSWA) and linear temperature decay (LTD). It can alleviate long-distance collapse problems and achieve longer text generation with a flexible trade-off between performance and inference speedup. Experiments on the storytelling and multi-paragraph opinionated article writing tasks show that pre-trained MLMs can achieve more than $3 \times \to 13 \times$ speedup with better performance than strong AR models. Our code is available at GitHub†.

We fill this gap by first conducting a preliminary study to calibrate the potential and 
limitations of a pre-trained MLM, i.e., RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019)<sup>†</sup>, on two story 
generation corpora, i.e., ROCStories (ROC) (Mostafazadeh et1al., 2016) and WritingPrompts (WP) 
(Fan et al., 2018). To achieve conditional generation, we simply use RoBERTa as both the encoder 
and the decoder with mixed attention (He et al., 2018) to achieve encoder-decoder cross-attention. 
Through experiments, we found that: (1) pre-trained MLMs can achieve competitive performance 
in the iterative NAR fashion for open-ended short text generation (e.g., a paragraph with around 
40 tokens), (2) pre-trained MLMs fail to model Open-LTG (with about 140 tokens on average), 
which will generate uninformative content with high-frequency and repeated tokens (e.g., “,” and 
“.”). Furthermore, we offer three possible reasons for the attention mechanism of MLMs and 
inference strategy to explain the collapse of the iterative NAR model based on pre-trained MLMs 
for the Open-LTG scenario.

Inspired by the above observations, we introduce two improvement strategies: Dynamic Sliding 
Window Attention (DSWA) and linear temperature decay strategy (LTD) to maintain more 
informative context content in the iterative NAR generation. As a result, iterative NAR models 
based on pre-trained MLMs can achieve much longer text generation than the vanilla setting. 
Experiments on two Open-LTG tasks (i.e., storytelling and multi-paragraph opinionated article 
writing) with four widely-used datasets demonstrate that the pre-trained MLM can achieve better 
performance (BLEU score, ROUGE score, BERT score, and Perplexity) than multiple strong AR 
models without extra post-training, structure modification, or using more model parameters. 
Importantly, our approach can speed up the inference process due to non-autoregressive properties, 
making the pre-trained MLM as a promising candidate for the Open-LTG community. The RoBERTa 
base achieves more than  $3 \times \rightarrow 13 \times$  with better performance to the competitive BART.

This paper explores Open-LTG with NAR models based on pre-trained MLMs. We first examined 
the potential and limitations of MLMs along with the iterative NAR inference for open-ended text 
generation and observed that MLMs would collapse for Open-LTG. Through extensive study and 
analysis, we found the reason is the inappropriate attention mechanism and inference strategies, 
and introduced two simple strategies to alleviate such a problem, i.e., dynamic sliding window 
attention and linear temperature decay. Experiments demonstrate that our model achieves 
competitive performance and significant speedup. We hope our research can make pre-trained MLMs 
as new candidates for the Open-LTG community.

query.content: According to the paper titled Quantized Side Tuning: Fast and Memory-Efficient Tuning of Quantized Large Language Models, what were the key insights from the ablation studies regarding QST's components and settings?

ground_truth.content: Ablation studies revealed several key insights: The reduction factor 'r' (default 16) significantly impacts efficiency, with memory footprint and FLOPS per token decreasing drastically when 'r' varies from 2 to 16, while MMLU accuracy changes only slightly. The NF4 data type proved superior, improving average accuracy by approximately 0.8% compared to FP4, leading to its adoption as the default 4-bit data type. Regarding computation data types, QST maintained similar performance with both BF16 and FP16, whereas QLoRA became unstable and failed on certain GLUE datasets (MRPC and QNLI for OPT-6.7B) when using FP16. Finally, Adapter was identified as the most effective downsample module, achieving the best performance and reducing trainable parameters and memory footprint compared to Linear, LoRA, MaxPooling, and AvgPooling.
references:
**Effects of reduction factor  $r$ .** We conduct experiments using LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-2-13B, and LLaMA-2-70B to verify the effects of reduction factor  $r$  (from 2 to 64) on memory footprint, MMLU accuracy, and throughput. We set the batch size to 4 and the sequence length to 384. The MMLU accuracy changes slightly as  $r$  varies as shown in Figure 5a. QST achieves the best accuracy of finetuning LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B when  $r$  is set to 16. As shown in Figure 5b and 5c, the memory footprint and the FLOPS per token decrease
drastically when  $r$  varies from 2 to 16 for finetuning all the models. The memory footprint and the FLOPS per token decrease slightly when  $r$  varies from 16 to 64. Therefore, we use  $r$  to 16 in our experiments as default.

**Effects of 4-bit data types.** We evaluate two 4-bit data types: FP4 and NF4 using the LLaMA-2 model series and the MMLU benchmark. As shown in Table 4, NF4 improves the average accuracy by about 0.8% compared with FP4. Therefore, we use NF4 as the default 4-bit data type in our experiments.

#### Effects of computation data types.

We analyze the effects of two computation data types: BF16 (results shown in Table 1) and FP16 (results shown in Table 5). As can be seen, QST retains similar results using FP16 and BF16. On the other hand, QLoRA is unstable using FP16 as the computation data type. We finetune OPT-6.7B on the GLUE benchmark and discover that QLoRA fails to finetune on the MRPC and QNLI datasets. We run each dataset under three different random seeds and QLoRA fails on two of them.

**Effects of downsample modules.** We conduct experiments on different downsample modules: Linear, LoRA, Adapter, MaxPooling, and AvgPooling using LLaMA-2-7B and the MMLU benchmark. As shown in Table 6, using Adapter as the downsample module achieves the best performance among all baselines, and reduces the trainable parameters and memory footprint.

query.content: According to the paper titled Sliding Windows Are Not the End: Exploring Full Ranking with Long-Context Large Language Models, what are the key experimental findings regarding the effectiveness and efficiency of the full ranking strategy compared to the sliding window strategy, including the impact of the proposed importance-aware loss?

ground_truth.content: Key experimental findings include: the fine-tuned full ranking model (RankMistral<sub>100</sub>) achieves superior performance (e.g., NDCG@10 of ~72.5) and significantly reduces latency (e.g., ~4.5s vs. ~6.5s) compared to the fine-tuned sliding window model (RankMistral<sub>20</sub>) on the TREC DL19 dataset, showing an absolute improvement of 2.2 in NDCG@10 and a 29.3% reduction in latency. In the supervised fine-tuning setting, RankMistral<sub>100</sub> outperforms RankMistral<sub>20</sub>, with an average improvement of about 4 points on TREC and 2 points on BEIR. The full ranking strategy significantly improves efficiency, achieving approximately 42% on Qwen-2.5 and 65% on GPT-4o compared to the sliding window strategy, and an approximate 8x speed-up when outputting only the top-10 passage IDs. It also reduces API costs by about 50%. However, in the zero-shot setting, the full ranking strategy generally underperforms the sliding window strategy. The proposed importance-aware loss ($L_{ia}$) enhances ranking effectiveness, with models dropping about 0.7 points on BEIR Avg without it, and RankMistral<sub>100</sub> generalizes well across different numbers of passages.
references: Surprisingly, our experiments reveal that full ranking with long-context LLMs can deliver superior performance in the supervised fine-tuning setting with a huge efficiency improvement. Furthermore, we identify two limitations of fine-tuning the full ranking model based on existing methods: (1) the sliding window strategy fails to produce a full ranking list as a training label, and (2) the language modeling loss cannot emphasize top-ranked passage IDs in the label. To alleviate these issues, we propose a complete listwise label construction approach and a novel importance-aware learning objective for full ranking. Experiments show the superior performance of our method over baselines. Our codes are available at <https://github.com/RUC-NLP/IR/FullRank>.

Figure 1: The sliding window strategy and full ranking strategy are shown in part (a) and part (b), respectively. The bar chart shows the comparison between our fine-tuned sliding window model and full ranking model in terms of NDCG@10 and latency (per query) on the TREC DL19 dataset.

Figure 1 shows the advantage of our fine-tuned full ranking model compared to the sliding window model: an absolute improvement of 2.2 in terms of NDCG@10 and a reduction in latency by 29.3% on the TREC DL19 dataset.

**Zero-shot** In the zero-shot setting, the full ranking strategy underperforms the sliding window strategy on nearly all datasets across all long-context LLMs. This demonstrates that full ranking significantly increases the ranking difficulty of LLM, resulting in a performance drop.

**Supervised Fine-tuning** In supervised fine-tuning setting, we find that our full ranking model RankMistral<sub>100</sub> outperforms sliding window model RankMistral<sub>20</sub> on nearly all datasets. Notably, RankMistral<sub>100</sub> achieves an average improvement of about 4 and 2 points on TREC and BEIR, respectively, compared to RankMistral<sub>20</sub> when fine-tuned from GPT-4o-mini. These results indicate that task-specific fine-tuning can help the full ranking model better model the global interaction between all the passages, thus yielding better ranking performance than the sliding window model.

Furthermore, we conduct an ablation study on RankMistral<sub>20</sub> and RankMistral<sub>100</sub> to prove the effectiveness of our importance-aware loss  $L_{ia}$  . Both models are fine-tuned from GPT-4o and trained with standard language modeling loss. The results are shown in part “w/o  $L_{ia}$  (SFT from GPT-4o)”. After removing  $L_{ia}$  , both RankMistral<sub>20</sub> and RankMistral<sub>100</sub> drop about 0.7 points on BEIR Avg, proving that  $L_{ia}$  makes the model focus more on top-ranked passage IDs, thereby enhancing its ranking effectiveness. Besides, even trained with standard language modeling loss, RankMistral<sub>100</sub> still outperforms RankMistral<sub>20</sub> on dl19, dl20, and BEIR Avg, which further demonstrates the effectiveness advantage of RankMistral<sub>100</sub> in supervised fine-tuning setting.

(1) Ranking latency of full ranking strategy (light orange bar) is much smaller than sliding window strategy (light green bar) across all long-context LLMs. For example, on the Signal dataset, the full ranking strategy achieves an efficiency improvement of approximately 42% on Qwen-2.5 and 65% on GPT-4o compared to the sliding window strategy. This demonstrates that the full ranking strategy is more efficient than the sliding window strategy.
(2) When the models are restricted to output only the top-10 passage IDs, both strategies (dark green bar and dark orange bar) demonstrate significant latency reduction, indicating that the number of decoded tokens greatly impacts the overall latency. Furthermore, the latency gap between the two strategies becomes even more pronounced. For example, on the Signal dataset, the sliding window strategy takes 29.9 seconds, while the full ranking strategy only takes 3.8 seconds, resulting in an approximate 8x speed-up. This highlights the efficiency advantage of the full ranking strategy in real-world search engines, where only the top 10 results need to be displayed after a user submits a query.

From the results, it can be seen that RankMistral<sub>100</sub> performs better than RankMistral<sub>20</sub> across differ-ent  $N$  values. This indicates that even though RankMistral<sub>100</sub> is trained on passage lists of length 100, it can still generalize to variable-length ranking tasks.
As shown in Figure 5, the full ranking strategy reduces API costs by about 50% compared to the sliding window strategy, which proves its cost-efficiency.

query.content: According to the paper titled The Internal State of an LLM Knows When It's Lying, summarize the main contributions.

ground_truth.content: The paper's main contributions are the release of a true-false statement dataset along with a method for generating such information, and demonstrating that an LLM's internal state can reveal the truthfulness of statements it reads or generates, proposing SAPLMA as a method to extract this information.

query.content: According to the paper titled Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts, what specific language models, including their architectural types and key characteristics, were analyzed in the study?

ground_truth.content: The study analyzed a diverse set of language models, including decoder-only models such as MPT-30B-Instruct (using ALiBi), LongChat-13B (16K) (an extended LLaMA-13B with condensed rotary positional embeddings), OpenAI’s GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K), Anthropic’s Claude-1.3 and Claude-1.3 (100K), and GPT-4 (8K). It also investigated encoder-decoder models like Flan-T5-XXL and Flan-UL2 (both using relative positional embeddings). Additionally, base models like MPT-30B and various Llama-2 models (7B, 13B, 70B, and their chat-fine-tuned versions) were examined to understand the effects of instruction fine-tuning and model scale.
references: We empirically investigate this question via controlled experiments with a variety of state-of-the-art open (MPT-30B-Instruct, LongChat-13B (16K)) and closed (OpenAI’s GPT-3.5-Turbo and Anthropic’s Claude-1.3) language models in settings that require accessing and using information within an input context.

**Open Models.** We experiment with MPT-30B-Instruct, which has a maximum context length of 8192 tokens. The model was initially pre-trained on 1 trillion tokens using 2048-token sequences, followed by an additional sequence length adaptation pre-training phase on 50 billion tokens using 8192-token sequences. MPT-30B-Instruct uses ALiBi (Press et al., 2022) to represent positional information. We also evaluate LongChat-13B (16K) (Li et al., 2023), which extends the LLaMA-13B (Touvron et al., 2023a) context window from 2048 to 16384 tokens by using condensed rotary positional embeddings before fine-tuning with 16384-token sequences.

**Closed Models.** We use the OpenAI API to experiment with GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K).<sup>5</sup> GPT-3.5-Turbo has a maximum context length of 4K tokens, and GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) is a version with an extended maximum context length of 16K tokens. We evaluate Claude-1.3 and Claude-1.3 (100K) with the Anthropic API; Claude-1.3 has a maximum context length of 8K tokens, and Claude-1.3 (100K) has an extended context length of 100K tokens.<sup>6</sup>
<sup>6</sup>We also evaluate GPT-4 (8K) on a subset of multi-document QA experiments, finding similar results and trends as other models (though GPT-4 has higher absolute performance).

The open models we evaluated are all decoder-only models—at each timestep, they may only attend to prior tokens. To better understand the potential effects of model architecture on how language model use context, we compare decoder-only and encoder-decoder language models.
We experiment with Flan-T5-XXL (Raffel et al., 2020; Chung et al., 2022) and Flan-UL2 (Tay et al., 2023). Flan-T5-XXL is trained with a sequences of 512 tokens (encoder and decoder). Flan-UL2 is initially trained with sequences of 512 tokens (encoder and decoder), but is then pre-trained for an extra 100K steps with 1024 tokens (encoder and decoder) before instruction fine-tuning on sequences with 2048 tokens in the encoder and 512 tokens in the decoder. However, since these models use relative positional embeddings, they can (in principle) extrapolate beyond
these maximum context lengths; Shaham et al. (2023) find that both models can perform well with sequences of up to 8K tokens.

To better understand the potential effects of instruction fine-tuning on how language models use long input contexts, we compare the multi-document question answering performance of MPT-30B-Instruct against its base model (i.e., before instruction fine-tuning) MPT-30B. We use the same experimental setup as §2.

We evaluate Llama-2 (Touvron et al., 2023b) on multi-document QA with 20 total documents in each input context. The Llama tokenizer produces longer sequences than the tokenizers for our previously-studied models, so we discard 20 examples (out of 2655) that exceed Llama-2’s maximum context length of 4096 tokens. We experiment with models of varying sizes (7B, 13B, and 70B parameters), with and without additional
supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback (“-chat-” models).

query.content: According to the paper titled Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering, describe the main components of the Dense Passage Retriever (DPR) model architecture and its training objective.

ground_truth.content: The Dense Passage Retriever (DPR) employs a simple dual-encoder framework. It consists of a Passage Encoder (E_P) and a Question Encoder (E_Q), both implemented using independent BERT (base, uncased) networks, where the [CLS] token's representation forms a 768-dimensional vector. The similarity between question and passage vectors is defined by their dot product. For efficient inference, all passages are indexed offline using FAISS. The training objective is to optimize a negative log likelihood loss, maximizing the log likelihood of the positive passage among a set of positive and negative passages in a batch. This training leverages "in-batch negatives" (where other positive passages in the batch serve as negatives) and optionally includes additional "hard" negative passages retrieved by BM25.
references:
Our dense passage retriever (DPR) uses a dense encoder  $E_P(\cdot)$  which maps any text passage to a  $d$ -dimensional real-valued vectors and builds an index for all the  $M$  passages that we will use for retrieval.

At run-time, DPR applies a different encoder  $E_Q(\cdot)$  that maps the input question to a  $d$ -dimensional vector, and retrieves  $k$  passages of which vectors are the closest to the question vector. We define the similarity between the question and the passage using the dot product of their vectors:

$$\text{sim}(q, p) = E_Q(q)^T E_P(p). \quad (1)$$

**Encoders** Although in principle the question and passage encoders can be implemented by any neural networks, in this work we use two independent BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) networks (base, uncased) and take the representation at the [CLS] token as the output, so  $d = 768$  .

**Inference** During inference time, we apply the passage encoder  $E_P$  to all the passages and index them using FAISS (Johnson et al., 2017) offline. FAISS is an extremely efficient, open-source library for similarity search and clustering of dense vectors, which can easily be applied to billions of vectors. Given a question  $q$  at run-time, we derive its embedding  $v_q = E_Q(q)$  and retrieve the top  $k$  passages with embeddings closest to  $v_q$  .

Training the encoders so that the dot-product similarity (Eq. (1)) becomes a good ranking function for retrieval is essentially a *metric learning* problem (Kulis, 2013). The goal is to create a vector space such that relevant pairs of questions and passages will have smaller distance (i.e., higher simi-larity) than the irrelevant ones, by learning a better embedding function.

Let  $\mathcal{D} = \{(q_i, p_i^+, p_{i,1}^-, \dots, p_{i,n}^-)\}_{i=1}^m$  be the training data that consists of  $m$  instances. Each instance contains one question  $q_i$  and one relevant (positive) passage  $p_i^+$  , along with  $n$  irrelevant (negative) passages  $p_{i,j}^-$  . We optimize the loss function as the negative log likelihood of the positive passage:

$$\begin{aligned} L(q_i, p_i^+, p_{i,1}^-, \dots, p_{i,n}^-) \ = -\log \frac{e^{\text{sim}(q_i, p_i^+)}}{e^{\text{sim}(q_i, x_i^+)} + \sum_{j=1}^{n} e^{\text{sim}(q_i, x_{i,j}^-)}}. \end{aligned} \quad (2)$$

**Positive and negative passages** For retrieval problems, it is often the case that positive examples are available explicitly, while negative examples need to be selected from an extremely large pool. ... Our best model uses gold passages from the same mini-batch and one BM25 negative passage. In particular, re-using gold passages from the same batch as negatives can make the computation efficient while achieving great performance. We discuss this approach below.

**In-batch negatives** Assume that we have  $B$  questions in a mini-batch and each one is associated with a relevant passage. Let  $\mathbf{Q}$  and  $\mathbf{P}$  be the  $(B \times d)$  matrix of question and passage embeddings in a batch of size  $B$  .  $\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{P}^T$  is a  $(B \times B)$  matrix of similarity scores, where each row of which corresponds to a question, paired with  $B$  passages. In this way, we reuse computation and effectively train on  $B^2$   $(q_i, p_j)$  question/passage pairs in each batch. Any  $(q_i, p_j)$  pair is a positive example when  $i = j$  , and negative otherwise. This creates  $B$  training instances in each batch, where there are  $B - 1$  negative passages for each question.

query.content: According to the paper titled Quantized Side Tuning: Fast and Memory-Efficient Tuning of Quantized Large Language Models, what are the primary performance and efficiency findings of QST compared to baselines?

ground_truth.content: The primary experimental findings demonstrate that QST significantly enhances efficiency. It reduces the total memory footprint by up to 2.3 $\times$ and speeds up the finetuning process by up to 3 $\times$ compared to state-of-the-art methods. When compared to full finetuning, QST achieves up to a 7 $\times$ reduction in total memory footprint. For instance, on OPT-1.3B and OPT-2.7B, QST reduces memory by around 2 $\times$ compared to QLoRA, LoRA, and Adapter, and trainable parameters by around 10 $\times$ and 5 $\times$ respectively. For OPT-6.7B, QST reduces memory footprint and trainable parameters by 2.3 $\times$ and 5.5 $\times$ compared to QLoRA, with only a 1.3% accuracy drop. On the MMLU benchmark, QST improves accuracy by 0.1% on average while reducing memory footprint by 1.8 $\times$ compared to QLoRA, with a 2.1% accuracy enhancement for LLaMA-2-13B. QST also achieves the lowest FLOPS per token, demonstrating around 2.5 $\times$ speed up compared to baselines. For LLaMA-2-70B chatbot finetuning, QST speeds up training by 3.2 $\times$ and reduces memory footprint by 1.7 $\times$ compared to QLoRA-70B, while improving the MT-Bench score by 0.46, and even outperforming the original LLaMA-2-70B by 0.21.
references: Experiments show that QST can reduce the total memory footprint by up to 2.3 $\times$  and speed up the finetuning process by up to 3 $\times$  while achieving competent performance compared with the state-of-the-art. When it comes to full finetuning, QST can reduce the total memory footprint up to 7 $\times$ .

Figure 1 compares the memory footprint of QST and existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, including QLoRA and LST.

To validate the effectiveness of our QST, we conduct extensive evaluations for different types of LLMs (e.g., OPT, LLaMA 2), with 1.3B to 70B parameters, on various benchmarks. Experiment results show that QST can reduce the total memory footprint by up to  $2.3 \times$  and speed up the finetuning process by up to  $3 \times$  while achieving competent performance compared with the state-of-the-art. Our codes are released to the GitHub<sup>1</sup>.

Overall, QST achieves the lowest memory footprint among all methods while attaining competent accuracy. Particularly, for relatively small models (i.e., OPT-1.3B and OPT-2.7B), QST re-
duces the memory footprint by around  $2\times$  compared with QLoRA, LoRA, and Adapter, while achieving comparable accuracy. Compared with LST, QST reduces the memory requirement by 3.2GB and 6.3GB for finetuning OPT-1.3B and OPT-2.7B. QST also reduces the trainable parameters by around  $10\times$  and  $5\times$  compared with QLoRA and the other baselines, respectively.

For larger models such as OPT-6.7B, we focus on comparing QST with QLoRA. This is because QLoRA has similar accuracy with the other baselines, but LoRA, Adapter, and LST all have excessively huge memory footprints of weights when it comes to finetuning OPT-6.7B<sup>2</sup>. Compared with QLoRA, QST reduces the memory footprint and trainable parameters by  $2.3\times$  and  $5.5\times$ , while only introducing a 1.3% accuracy drop.

QST improves the accuracy by 0.1% on average while reducing the memory footprint by 1.8 $\times$  compared with QLoRA. Particularly, QST yields an enhancement of 2.1% in accuracy over QLoRA when finetuning LLaMA-2-13B. When finetuning the OPT-2.7B, OPT-6.7B, and OPT-13B models, QST achieves 0.3%, 0.6%, and 0.3% accuracy improvements, respectively.

Table 3 shows the training throughput of different methods, measured by FLOPS per token (the lower the better), on LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-2-13B, and LLaMA-2-70B. While the FLOPS per token of all methods increases as the model size grows, QST achieves the lowest FLOPS per token among all. Particularly, QST achieves around  $2.5\times$  speed up compared with the baselines. LST suffers from the highest FLOPS per token. The FLOPS per token of QLoRA is slightly higher than LoRA and Adapter since QLoRA adds more LoRA components.

Table 7 shows the experiment results of QLoRA and QST on the total training time, memory footprint, and the average MT-Bench score over 8 categories. QST speeds up the training by  $3.2 \times$  and reduces memory footprint by  $1.7 \times$ , with even an improved score of 0.46 compared with QLoRA. Notably, QST’s chatbot performance outperforms the original LLaMA-2-70B, achieving an improvement of 0.21.

query.content: According to the paper titled The Internal State of an LLM Knows When It's Lying, describe all datasets used in the research.

ground_truth.content: The paper utilized two main datasets: a custom 'true-false dataset' comprising 6,084 sentences from 6 diverse topics (Cities, Inventions, Chemical Elements, Animals, Companies, Scientific Facts) for training and testing truthfulness classification, and a dataset of 245 manually labeled sentences generated by the OPT-6.7b LLM itself, also used for truthfulness classification.
references:
The work presented in this paper requires a dataset of true and false statements. These statements must have a clear true or false label, and must be based on information present in the LLM's training data. Furthermore, since our approach intends to reveal that the hidden states of an LLM have a notion of a statement being true or false, the dataset must cover several disjoint topics, such that a classifier can be trained on the LLM's activations of some topics while being tested on another. Unfortunately, we could not find any such dataset and therefore, compose the true-false dataset.

Our true-false dataset covers the following topics: "Cities", "Inventions", "Chemical Elements", "Animals", "Companies", and "Scientific Facts".

For the first 5 topics, we used the following method to compose the dataset. We used a reliable source<sup>1</sup> that included a table with several properties for each instance. For example, for the "chemical elements" we used a table that included, for each element, its name, atomic number, symbol, standard state, group block, and a unique property (e.g., Hydrogen, 1, H, Gas, Nonmetal, the most abundant element in the universe). For each element we composed true statement using the element name and one of its properties (e.g., "The atomic number of Hydrogen is 1"). Then, we randomly selected a different row for composing a false statement (e.g., "The atomic number of Hydrogen is 34"). If the value in the different row is identical to the value in the current row, we resample a different row until we obtain a value that is different. This process was repeated for the all topics except the "Scientific Facts". For the "Scientific Facts" topic, we asked ChatGPT (Feb 13 version) to provide "scientific facts that are well known to humans" (e.g. "The sky is often cloudy when it's going to rain"). We then asked ChatGPT to provide the opposite of each statement such that it becomes a false statement (e.g., "The sky is often clear when it's going to rain"). The statements provided by ChatGPT were manually curated, and verified by two human annotators. The classification of 48 facts were questioned by at least one of the annotators; these facts were removed from the dataset. The true-false dataset comprises 6,084 sentences, including 1,458 sentences for "Cities", 876 for "Inventions", 930 for "Chemical Elements", 1,008 for "Animals", 1,200 for "Companies", and 612 for "Scientific Facts".

In addition to the topics from the true-false dataset, we also created a second data set of statements generated by the LLM itself (the OPT-6.7b model). For generating statements, we provided a true statement not present in the dataset, and allowed the LLM to generate a following statement. We first filtered out any statements that were not factual statements (e.g., “I’m not familiar with the Japanese versions of the games.”). All statements were generated using the most probable next word at each step, i.e., we did not use sampling. This resulted in 245 labeled statements. The statements were fact-checked and manually labeled by three human judges based on web-searches. The human judges had a very high average observed agreement of 97.82%, and an average Cohen’s Kappa of 0.9566. The majority determined the ground-truth label for each statement. 48.6% of the statements were labeled as true, resulting in a balanced dataset.

query.content: According to the paper titled Sliding Windows Are Not the End: Exploring Full Ranking with Long-Context Large Language Models, describe the core model architecture components and the specific techniques proposed for fine-tuning the full ranking model.

ground_truth.content: The backbone model for fine-tuning is Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3. The paper proposes two specific techniques for fine-tuning the full ranking model: a Multi-pass Sliding Window Approach, which iteratively generates a complete full ranking list as a training label by applying the sliding window strategy multiple times (e.g., ranking 100 passages, then the remaining 90, and so on); and an Importance-Aware Learning Objective ($L_{\text{ia}}$), which includes a position-based weight $w_p$ to reweight the importance of each passage ID in the label, ensuring higher-ranked passage IDs receive greater weight during loss calculation. The loss function is defined as $L_{\text{ia}} = - \sum_{i=1}^{|y|} w_i \log(P_{\theta}(y_i | x, y_{<i}))$, where $w_i = \begin{cases} 1 + \frac{1}{\log_2(p_i+1)}, & i \in \text{passage IDs}, \\ \alpha, & i \notin \text{passage IDs}. \end{cases}$
references: We choose Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 as our backbone model and use two different teacher models: GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o. The finetuned full ranking model and sliding window model are denoted as **RankMistral100** and **RankMistral20**, respectively. Both models are optimized with our proposed importance-aware loss for fair comparison.

To address these limitations, we design a multi-pass sliding window approach to generate high-quality full ranking lists as training labels and propose a novel importance-aware learning objective for model optimization. Next, we will introduce the details of our methods.

To generate the full ranking list for model fine-tuning, we first employ BM25 to retrieve the top-100 candidate passages, which are then reranked using a teacher model. In theory, a single pass of the sliding window process (ranking from back to front with a window size of 20 and a stride of 10) can only ensure the retrieval of the top 10 most relevant passages. To overcome this limitation, we propose a multi-pass sliding window approach to obtain the full ranking list, as illustrated in Figure 2. In the first pass, the sliding window strategy is applied to rerank all 100 passages, yielding the top 10 most relevant passages. In the second pass, the same strategy is used to rerank the remaining 90 passages, producing the next 10 most relevant passages. This iterative process continues until the entire reranked list is constructed.

To address this issue, we propose an importance-aware loss function  $L_{\text{ia}}$  which includes a position-based weight  $w_p$  to reweight the importance of each passage ID in the label. The  $L_{\text{ia}}$  is defined as:
$$L_{\text{ia}} = - \sum_{i=1}^{|y|} w_i \log(P_{\theta}(y_i | x, y_{<i})), \quad (2)$$
$$w_i = \begin{cases} 1 + \frac{1}{\log_2(p_i+1)}, & i \in \text{passage IDs}, \\ \alpha, & i \notin \text{passage IDs}. \end{cases} \quad (3)$$
Here,  $p_i$  represents the passage rank corresponding to the  $i$ -th token. Note that each passage ID will be split into multiple tokens (e.g., [99]) will be split into “[”, “9”, “9”, and “]”), and these tokens have the same weight.<sup>1</sup> Besides, we believe that the importance of passage IDs is higher than that of relational operator “>”, so we set the weight of “>” as  $\alpha$  ( $\alpha < 1$ ). By incorporating the importance-aware loss  $L_{\text{ia}}$  , we ensure that higher-ranked passage IDs receive greater weight during loss calculation, which better aligns with the training of the full-ranking model.

query.content: According to the paper titled TinyBERT: Distilling BERT for Natural Language Understanding, describe the model architecture components of TinyBERT, detailing its structure, the teacher model, and the key techniques used for Transformer distillation.

ground_truth.content:
TinyBERT is a Transformer-based student model. TinyBERT<sub>4</sub> has 4 layers ( $M=4$ ), a hidden size of  $d'=312$ , a feed-forward/filter size of  $d'_f=1200$ , and 12 attention heads ( $h=12$ ), totaling 14.5M parameters. TinyBERT<sub>6</sub> has 6 layers ( $M=6$ ), a hidden size of  $d'=768$ , a feed-forward/filter size of  $d'_i=3072$ , and 12 attention heads ( $h=12$ ), totaling 67.0M parameters. The teacher model is BERT<sub>BASE</sub>, which has 12 layers ( $N=12$ ), a hidden size of  $d=768$ , a feed-forward size of  $d_i=3072$ , and 12 attention heads ( $h=12$ ), with 109M parameters. A layer mapping function, such as  $g(m) = 3 \times m$  for TinyBERT<sub>4</sub>, defines which student layer learns from which teacher layer.

The key techniques for Transformer distillation include:
1.  **Attention-based Distillation ( $\mathcal{L}_{\text{attn}}$ ):** Uses Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss to fit the unnormalized attention matrices ( $\mathbf{A}_i^S$ ) of the student to those of the teacher ( $\mathbf{A}_i^T$ ).
2.  **Hidden States-based Distillation ( $\mathcal{L}_{\text{hidn}}$ ):** Uses MSE loss to fit the hidden states of the student ( $\mathbf{H}^S$ ) to those of the teacher ( $\mathbf{H}^T$ ), incorporating a learnable linear transformation  $\mathbf{W}_h$  to match dimensions.
3.  **Embedding-layer Distillation ( $\mathcal{L}_{\text{embd}}$ ):** Uses MSE loss to fit the student's embeddings ( $\mathbf{E}^S$ ) to the teacher's ( $\mathbf{E}^T$ ), also with a linear transformation  $\mathbf{W}_e$ .
4.  **Prediction-layer Distillation ( $\mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}}$ ):** Uses soft cross-entropy (CE) loss to penalize the difference between the student's logits ( $\mathbf{z}^S$ ) and the teacher's logits ( $\mathbf{z}^T$ ), with a temperature value  $t=1$ .
references:
We instantiate a tiny student model (the number of layers  $M=4$ , the hidden size  $d'=312$ , the feed-forward/filter size  $d'_f=1200$  and the head number  $h=12$ ) that has a total of 14.5M parameters. This model is referred to as TinyBERT<sub>4</sub>. The original
BERT<sub>BASE</sub> ( $N=12$ ,  $d=768$ ,  $d_i=3072$  and  $h=12$ ) is used as the teacher model that contains 109M parameters. We use  $g(m) = 3 \times m$  as the layer mapping function, so TinyBERT<sub>4</sub> learns from every 3 layers of BERT<sub>BASE</sub>. The learning weight  $\lambda$  of each layer is set to 1. Besides, for a direct comparisons with baselines, we also instantiate a TinyBERT<sub>6</sub> ( $M=6$ ,  $d'=768$ ,  $d'_i=3072$  and  $h=12$ ) with the same architecture as BERT<sub>6</sub>-PKD (Sun et al., 2019) and DistilBERT<sub>6</sub> (Sanh et al., 2019).

**Transformer-layer Distillation.** The proposed Transformer-layer distillation includes the *attention based distillation* and *hidden states based distillation*, which is shown in Figure 2. The attention based distillation is motivated by the recent findings that attention weights learned by BERT can capture rich linguistic knowledge (Clark et al., 2019). This kind of linguistic knowledge includes the syntax and coreference information, which is essential for natural language understanding. Thus we propose the attention based distillation to encourage that the linguistic knowledge can be transferred from teacher (BERT) to student (TinyBERT). Specifically, the student learns to fit the matrices of multi-head attention in the teacher network, and the objective is defined as:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{attn}} = \frac{1}{h} \sum_{i=1}^{h} \text{MSE}(\mathbf{A}_i^S, \mathbf{A}_i^T), \quad (7)$$

where  $h$  is the number of attention heads,  $\mathbf{A}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{l \times l}$  refers to the attention matrix corresponding to the  $i$ -th head of teacher or student,  $l$  is the input text length, and  $\text{MSE}(\cdot)$  means the *mean squared error* loss function. In this work, the (unnormalized) attention matrix  $\mathbf{A}_i$  is used as the fitting target instead of its softmax output  $\text{softmax}(\mathbf{A}_i)$ , since our experiments show that the former setting has a faster convergence rate and better performances.

In addition to the attention based distillation, we also distill the knowledge from the output of Transformer layer, and the objective is as follows:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{hidn}} = \text{MSE}(\mathbf{H}^S \mathbf{W}_h, \mathbf{H}^T), \quad (8)$$

where the matrices  $\mathbf{H}^S \in \mathbb{R}^{l \times d'}$  and  $\mathbf{H}^T \in \mathbb{R}^{l \times d}$  refer to the hidden states of student and teacher networks respectively, which are calculated by Equation 4. The scalar values  $d$  and  $d'$  denote the hidden sizes of teacher and student models, and  $d'$  is often smaller than  $d$  to obtain a smaller student network. The matrix  $\mathbf{W}_h \in \mathbb{R}^{d' \times d}$  is a learnable linear transformation, which transforms the hidden states of student network into the same space as the teacher network's states.

**Embedding-layer Distillation.** Similar to the hidden states based distillation, we also perform embedding-layer distillation and the objective is:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{embd}} = \text{MSE}(\mathbf{E}^S \mathbf{W}_e, \mathbf{E}^T), \quad (9)$$

where the matrices  $\mathbf{E}^S$  and  $\mathbf{H}^T$  refer to the embeddings of student and teacher networks, respectively. In this paper, they have the same shape as the hidden state matrices. The matrix  $\mathbf{W}_e$  is a linear transformation playing a similar role as  $\mathbf{W}_h$ .

**Prediction-layer Distillation.** In addition to imitating the behaviors of intermediate layers, we also use the knowledge distillation to fit the predictions of teacher model as in Hinton et al. (2015). Specifically, we penalize the soft cross-entropy loss between the student network's logits against the teacher's logits:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}} = \text{CE}(\mathbf{z}^T/t, \mathbf{z}^S/t), \quad (10)$$

where  $\mathbf{z}^S$  and  $\mathbf{z}^T$  are the logits vectors predicted by the student and teacher respectively,  $\text{CE}$  means the *cross entropy* loss, and  $t$  means the temperature value. In our experiment, we find that  $t = 1$  performs well.

Using the above distillation objectives (i.e. Equations 7, 8, 9 and 10), we can unify the distillation loss of the corresponding layers between the teacher and the student network:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{layer}} = \begin{cases} \mathcal{L}_{\text{embd}}, & m=0 \\ \mathcal{L}_{\text{hidn}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{attn}}, & M \ge m > 0 \\ \mathcal{L}_{\text{pred}}, & m = M + 1 \end{cases} \quad (11)$$

query.content: According to the paper titled The Impossibility of Fair LLMs, summarize the main contributions of this work.

ground_truth.content: The paper argues that fairness through unawareness of sensitive attributes is impossible for LLMs due to unstructured training data and limited transparency. It also states that standards for the fair treatment of content producers can be rendered obsolete by the LLM's capacity for large-scale content consumption and redistribution. Furthermore, general-purpose LLMs cannot be made fair across many contexts because of the diverse combinations of populations, use cases, and other factors that impose different fairness requirements. The paper also highlights that fairness does not compose, meaning LLM development and deployment involving the composition of different models each present their own fairness challenges. Lastly, it identifies important and tractable future work on LLM fairness, focusing on crafting standards of developer responsibility, refining in-depth methods for context-specific evaluation, and building scalable evaluations that iterate through participatory design and leverage AI capabilities to address the multitude of real-world contexts.
references:
Specifically, we make the

following arguments:

- Fairness through unawareness of sensitive attributes is made impossible by the unstructured training data and limited transparency of LLMs (Section 4.1).
- Standards for the fair treatment of content producers can be rendered obsolete by the LLM capacity for large-scale consumption and redistribution of content (Section 4.2).
- General-purpose LLMs cannot be made fair across many contexts because of the combinations of populations, use cases, and other factors that impose different fairness requirements (Section 4.3).
- Fairness does not compose, and LLM development and deployment involve the composition of different models, each with their own fairness challenges (Section 4.4).
- There is much important and tractable work to be done on LLM fairness, particularly in crafting standards of developer responsibility, refining in-depth methods for context-specific evaluation, and building scalable evaluations that iterate through participatory design and using AI capabilities to scale up to the multitude of real-world contexts (Section 5).

query.content: According to the paper titled The Impossibility of Fair LLMs, what were the key experimental findings?

ground_truth.content: As a conceptual and theoretical analysis, the paper does not present experimental findings. Instead, its key discoveries are conceptual arguments demonstrating that achieving fairness in general-purpose LLMs is intractable. The paper argues that fairness through unawareness is impossible by design due to unstructured training data and limited transparency. It also finds that producer-side fairness criteria can be rendered obsolete by LLMs' capacity for large-scale content consumption and redistribution. Furthermore, general-purpose LLMs cannot be made fair across many contexts due to the combinatorial complexity of populations, use cases, and factors imposing different fairness requirements. Finally, the paper concludes that fairness does not compose, meaning fairness guarantees for individual models do not extend to composed systems.
references: We analyze a variety of technical fairness frameworks and find inherent challenges in each that make the development of a fair LLM intractable. We show that each framework either does not logically extend to the general-purpose AI context or is infeasible in practice, primarily due to the large amounts of unstructured training data and the many potential combinations of human populations, use cases, and sensitive attributes.

We develop the stronger claim: fairness in the rigorous sense defined by these frameworks for narrow use, even on a single nontrivial metric, is intractable with general-purpose LLMs. The inherent challenges would persist regardless of advances in empirical methods, but we present future directions in light of them. Specifically, we make the

following arguments:

- Fairness through unawareness of sensitive attributes is made impossible by the unstructured training data and limited transparency of LLMs (Section 4.1).
- Standards for the fair treatment of content producers can be rendered obsolete by the LLM capacity for large-scale consumption and redistribution of content (Section 4.2).
- General-purpose LLMs cannot be made fair across many contexts because of the combinations of populations, use cases, and other factors that impose different fairness requirements (Section 4.3).
- Fairness does not compose, and LLM development and deployment involve the composition of different models, each with their own fairness challenges (Section 4.4).

The preceding claims and analysis were not developed mathematically, and the outcome of such analysis would depend on particular assumptions and operationalizations. It is also possible that compelling new technical frameworks, perhaps developed specifically for general-purpose LLMs or other general-purpose systems, will circumvent the inherent challenges we described. Finally, while we believe it is important to lay out a conceptual foundation of what is and is not possible, there are many open empirical challenges that we have not addressed in this work, particularly the quantification of how much fairness metrics can be partially satisfied in real-world settings and the development of scalable methods for context-specific alignment with fairness and other social values.

query.content: According to the paper titled Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts, what datasets were utilized for the multi-document question answering, open-domain question answering, and key-value retrieval tasks?

ground_truth.content: The paper utilized the NaturalQuestions-Open dataset for both multi-document question answering and open-domain question answering tasks. Additionally, a dataset of Synthetic Key-Value Pairs, consisting of randomly generated UUIDs, was used for the key-value retrieval task.
references: We first experiment with multi-document question answering, which requires models to reason over provided documents to find relevant information and use it to answer a given question; this task mimics the retrieval-augmented generation setup underlying many commercial generative search and question answering applications (e.g., Bing Chat).

We instantiate this task with data from NaturalQuestions-Open (Lee et al., 2019; Kwiatkowski et al., 2019), which contains historical queries issued to the Google search engine, coupled with human-annotated answers extracted from Wikipedia. In particular, we take the 2655 queries where the annotated long answer is a paragraph (as opposed to a list or a table). We use passages (chunks of at most 100 tokens) from Wikipedia as documents within our input contexts.

Given that language models struggle to retrieve and use relevant information in the multi-document question answering task, to what extent can language models even *retrieve* from their input contexts? We study this question with a synthetic key-value retrieval task, which is designed to be a minimal testbed for the basic ability to retrieve matching tokens from the input context. In this task, models are given a collection of JSON-formatted key-value pairs and must return the value associated with a specific key.

In our synthetic key-value retrieval task, the inputs are (i) a string-serialized JSON object with  $k$  key-value pairs, where each of the keys and values are unique, randomly generated UUIDs and (ii) a key within the aforementioned JSON object. The goal is to return the value associated with the specified key.

We use language models in a standard retriever-reader setup. A retrieval system (Contriever, fine-tuned on MS-MARCO) takes an input query from NaturalQuestions-Open and returns the  $k$  documents from Wikipedia with the highest relevance score. To condition language models on these retrieved documents, we simply include them in the prompt. We evaluate retriever recall and reader accuracy (whether any of the annotated answers appear in the predicted output) as a function of the number of retrieved documents  $k$  . We use a subset of NaturalQuestions-Open where the long answer is a paragraph (as opposed to a table or a list).

query.content: According to the paper titled GLUE: A Multi-Task Benchmark and Analysis Platform for Natural Language Understanding, what were the key experimental findings regarding model performance and the state of NLU?

ground_truth.content: Key experimental findings indicate that the best models still achieve fairly low absolute scores on the GLUE benchmark, and analysis with the diagnostic dataset yields similarly weak performance over all linguistic phenomena tested, with some exceptions. Experiments suggest that solving GLUE is beyond the capability of current transfer learning methods. Specifically, the Multi-task model achieved the highest average performance on the GLUE benchmark with a score of 69.0, outperforming Single-task models (64.8 Avg) and pretrained models like GenSen (66.6 Avg). Performance on the benchmark correlates with performance on the diagnostic data, and even the best baselines achieve low absolute performance on the linguistic phenomena in the diagnostic data.
references: We evaluate baselines that use ELMo (Peters *et al.*, 2018), a powerful transfer learning technique, as well as state-of-the-art sentence representation models. The best models still achieve fairly low absolute scores. Analysis with our diagnostic dataset yields similarly weak performance over all phenomena tested, with some exceptions.

We find that our models trained directly on the GLUE tasks generally outperform those that do not, though all models obtain fairly low absolute scores. Probing the baselines with the diagnostic data, we find that performance on the benchmark correlates with performance on the diagnostic data, and that the best baselines similarly achieve low absolute performance on the linguistic phenomena included in the diagnostic data.
Experiments indicate that solving GLUE is beyond the capability of current transfer learning methods.

query.content: According to the paper titled Sliding Windows Are Not the End: Exploring Full Ranking with Long-Context Large Language Models, what are the main contributions of this research?

ground_truth.content: The main contributions are: conducting the first comprehensive study of long-context LLMs for ranking tasks; revealing that in a zero-shot setting, full ranking with long-context models is more efficient but less effective than the sliding window strategy; and proposing a complete listwise label construction approach and a novel importance-aware learning objective for fine-tuning the full ranking model to enhance its effectiveness.
references:
- We conduct a comprehensive study of long-context LLMs for ranking. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to investigate the application of long-context LLMs in ranking tasks.
  - We reveal that, in a zero-shot setting, full ranking with long-context models is more efficient but less effective compared to the sliding window strategy.
  - To enhance the effectiveness of full ranking, we propose a complete listwise label construction approach and a novel importance-aware learning objective for fine-tuning the full ranking model.

query.content: What are the primary evaluation metrics used for tasks like SST-2 and QQP within the GLUE benchmark, and how does a 4-layer distilled BERT model perform on average across the GLUE benchmark?

ground_truth.content: For SST-2 and QQP, accuracy is a primary evaluation metric. A 4-layer distilled BERT model (TinyBERT<sub>4</sub>) achieves an average score of 77.0 on the GLUE test set.

query.content: What are the key techniques employed by TinyBERT and Quantized Side Tuning to make large language models more efficient?

ground_truth.content: TinyBERT employs a novel Transformer distillation method and a two-stage learning framework. The Transformer distillation involves three types of loss functions for the embedding layer, hidden states and attention matrices of Transformer layers, and the prediction layer logits. The two-stage learning framework includes general distillation on a large-scale text corpus and task-specific distillation on an augmented task-specific dataset. Quantized Side Tuning (QST) uses a dual-stage process: first, it quantizes an LLM’s model weights into 4-bit. Second, it introduces a separate side network that utilizes the hidden states of the LLM to make task-specific predictions, avoiding back-propagation through the LLM. QST also leverages low-rank adaptors and gradient-free downsample modules (like LoRA, Adapter, MaxPooling, and AvgPooling) to reduce trainable parameters and optimizer states.

query.content: What specific challenges do Quantized Side Tuning and Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation aim to overcome in the domain of large language models?

ground_truth.content:
Quantized Side Tuning (QST) aims to overcome the substantial memory demands and long training times associated with finetuning large language models (LLMs). Specifically, it addresses the memory footprint stemming from three contributors: model weights, optimizer states, and intermediate activations, which existing methods often fail to mitigate simultaneously. QST also tackles the limitations of Parameter-Efficient Finetuning (PEFT) methods that still require considerable memory for intermediate activations and the issue with QLoRA's inability to handle large batch sizes due to intermediate activation memory, leading to long training times. Furthermore, it seeks to extend memory-efficient finetuning to larger models (beyond 3 billion parameters), which prior side network approaches struggled with.

Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation (HYBGRAG) aims to solve the challenges in Hybrid Question Answering (HQA) over semi-structured knowledge bases (SKBs). The primary challenges are that many questions require a synergy of both textual and relational information (Challenge 1: Hybrid-Sourcing Question), which existing RAG or GRAG methods struggle with as they focus on only one modality. Additionally, LLMs often struggle to distinguish between the textual and relational aspects of hybrid questions on the first attempt, necessitating further refinements (Challenge 2: Refinement-Required Question).

query.content: How do different language model architectures, such as encoder-decoder models and masked language models, handle long input contexts or long text generation, and what are their respective challenges?

ground_truth.content: Encoder-decoder models like Flan-UL2 are relatively robust to changes in relevant information position within their training-time sequence length, showing only a 1.9% absolute difference between best- and worst-case performance. However, decoder-only models like GPT-3.5-Turbo can experience significant performance degradation (over 20%) when relevant information is in the middle of long contexts. Masked language models (MLMs) like RoBERTa, when adapted for open-ended long text generation, face a 'collapse problem' where they generate uninformative and repetitive content for texts around 140 tokens, requiring specific techniques like Dynamic Sliding Window Attention (DSWA) and Linear Temperature Decay (LTD) to alleviate long-distance collapse and improve sampling.

query.content: What specific large language models are mentioned in the context of evaluating their truthfulness and analyzing their fairness limitations?

ground_truth.content: For evaluating truthfulness, Facebook OPT-6.7b and LLAMA2-7b are used. For analyzing fairness limitations, general-purpose LLMs such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, GPT-4, and Llama are considered.

query.content: What large language models are utilized or evaluated for both memory-efficient finetuning and hybrid retrieval-augmented generation tasks?

ground_truth.content: For memory-efficient finetuning, models like the OPT series (OPT-1.3B, OPT-2.7B, OPT-6.7B, OPT-13B, OPT-30B, and OPT-66B) and the LLaMA-2 series (LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-2-13B, and LLaMA-2-70B) are utilized and evaluated on various benchmarks. For hybrid retrieval-augmented generation, LLMs such as Claude 3 Sonnet, Claude 3 Haiku, and Llama 3.1 70B are employed, with some baselines also using Claude 3 Opus.

query.content: How does increasing the input context length affect the performance of language models in tasks like question answering and text generation?

ground_truth.content: In multi-document question answering, increasing context length by providing more documents (e.g., from 20 to 50) only marginally improves performance (around 1-1.5% for GPT-3.5-Turbo and Claude-1.3), indicating that models struggle to effectively use additional retrieved information. For long text generation, autoregressive models like BART suffer from decreased inference efficiency with increased generation length, while non-autoregressive models enhanced with techniques like Dynamic Sliding Window Attention aim to maintain performance and efficiency for longer outputs.

query.content: What techniques are proposed to improve how language models handle or generate long texts and contexts?

ground_truth.content: To improve long text generation, techniques like Dynamic Sliding Window Attention (DSWA) are used to alleviate long-distance collapse by restricting attention to neighbor tokens, and Linear Temperature Decay (LTD) is applied to improve sampling effectiveness by adjusting confidence scores during iterative refinement. For improving context utilization in long inputs, query-aware contextualization can dramatically improve performance on retrieval tasks, and instruction fine-tuning can help mitigate positional biases, although it minimally affects multi-document QA trends.

query.content: What is the purpose of the GLUE benchmark, and how do distilled models like TinyBERT demonstrate progress in NLU capabilities on this benchmark?

ground_truth.content: The GLUE benchmark is a multi-task benchmark and analysis platform for Natural Language Understanding, designed to spur the development of generalizable NLU systems by evaluating models across nine diverse tasks. Distilled models like TinyBERT demonstrate progress by achieving high performance (e.g., TinyBERT<sub>4</sub> with 77.0 average score) on this benchmark while being significantly smaller and faster than their teacher models, addressing the computational expense challenge.

query.content: What are the primary challenges related to large model deployment and finetuning that TinyBERT and Quantized Side Tuning aim to solve?

ground_truth.content: TinyBERT aims to solve the challenges of computationally expensive pre-trained language models (PLMs) that have a large number of parameters and long inference times, making them difficult to deploy efficiently on resource-restricted devices like mobile phones. Quantized Side Tuning (QST) addresses the substantial memory demands of LLM finetuning, which typically stem from model weights, optimizer states, and intermediate activations. Existing methods often fail to mitigate the memory footprint from all three sources simultaneously, with finetuning a 16-bit LLaMA model with 65 billion parameters requiring over 780GB of memory.

query.content: How does the nature of training data contribute to the challenges of ensuring both factual accuracy and fairness in large language models?

ground_truth.content: The massive amounts of unstructured training data used by LLMs contribute to challenges in both factual accuracy (leading to hallucination) and fairness. Specifically, this unstructured data makes sensitive attributes readily inferable, rendering fairness through unawareness impossible and complicating debiasing efforts without distorting information for other contexts.

query.content: How do the speed improvements compare between the model distillation technique and the quantized side tuning method?

ground_truth.content: The model distillation technique, specifically TinyBERT<sub>4</sub>, achieves a 9.4x faster *inference* speed compared to its teacher BERT<sub>BASE</sub>. The quantized side tuning (QST) method, on the other hand, speeds up the *finetuning* process by up to 3x compared to state-of-the-art methods like QLoRA. For LLaMA-2-70B, QST speeds up training by 3.2x compared to QLoRA.

query.content: Do these studies present empirical performance metrics or conceptual arguments about LLM capabilities?

ground_truth.content: One study presents empirical performance metrics, such as accuracy and AUC, for its proposed truthfulness detection method (SAPLMA) on specific LLMs like OPT-6.7b and LLAMA2-7b. The other study presents conceptual arguments and theoretical analysis, concluding that fairness frameworks are intractable for general-purpose LLMs, without offering quantitative performance metrics.

query.content: How do the proposed methods enhance the practical utility or effectiveness of Large Language Models?

ground_truth.content:
QST enhances LLM utility by making their finetuning significantly more memory-efficient and faster. It addresses the substantial memory demands of LLM finetuning by simultaneously mitigating the memory footprint of model weights (through 4-bit quantization), optimizer states (through low-rank adaptors and gradient-free downsample modules), and intermediate activations (by avoiding back-propagation through the LLM using a side network). This enables the adaptation of large models (up to 70B parameters) in memory-constrained scenarios.

HYBGRAG improves LLM effectiveness by enabling them to answer complex 'hybrid' questions that require combining both textual and relational information from semi-structured knowledge bases (SKB), a task traditional RAG and GRAG methods struggle with. It achieves this through an adaptive, agentic, and interpretable self-reflective system that refines question routing and leverages a retriever bank for hybrid information retrieval.

query.content: Which aspects of LLM reliability and ethics are explored in these two studies?

ground_truth.content: One study focuses on the reliability aspect of LLMs, specifically their tendency to hallucinate and provide false information, and how to detect this. The other study focuses on the ethical aspect of LLMs, specifically the challenges and impossibility of achieving various definitions of fairness.

query.content: Which approach offers greater memory footprint reduction, the model distillation method or the quantized side tuning method?

ground_truth.content: The model distillation method (TinyBERT) focuses on reducing the *model size*, with TinyBERT<sub>4</sub> being 7.3x to 7.5x smaller than its teacher BERT<sub>BASE</sub>. The quantized side tuning (QST) method explicitly targets *total memory footprint reduction* during finetuning, achieving up to 2.3x reduction compared to state-of-the-art methods like QLoRA and up to 7x reduction compared to full finetuning for large language models. For instance, QST reduces the memory footprint by 1.8x compared to QLoRA on average.

query.content: How do the methods' performance metrics compare on their main evaluation tasks?

ground_truth.content:
QST's performance metrics vary across tasks. On the GLUE benchmark, for OPT-6.7B, QST achieves an average accuracy of 84.2% with a 1.3% accuracy drop compared to QLoRA (85.5%). On the MMLU 5-shot benchmark, QST shows an average accuracy improvement of 0.1% over QLoRA, with specific enhancements of 2.1% for LLaMA-2-13B (56.8% vs 54.7%) and 0.3-0.6% for OPT-2.7B, OPT-6.7B, and OPT-13B. For chatbot performance on MT-Bench with LLaMA-2-70B, QST-70B achieves a score of 7.07, outperforming QLoRA-70B (6.61) and the original LLaMA-2-70B (6.86).

HYBGRAG demonstrates strong performance on retrieval tasks. On the STARK-MAG benchmark, it achieves a Hit@1 of 0.6540, a Hit@5 of 0.7531, and an MRR of 0.6980, significantly outperforming the next best baseline (AVATAR) with a 47.4% relative improvement in Hit@1. On STARK-PRIME, HYBGRAG achieves a Hit@1 of 0.2856, a Hit@5 of 0.4138, and an MRR of 0.3449, showing a 54.9% relative improvement in Hit@1 over AVATAR. For end-to-end RAG evaluation on CRAG, HYBGRAG achieves a Score<sub>a</sub> of 0.1618 with Llama 3.1 70B and 0.3363 with Claude 3 Sonnet, consistently outperforming all baselines.

query.content: What types of language model architectures are primarily investigated in each study?

ground_truth.content: One study primarily investigates an encoder-based masked language model (RoBERTa) for non-autoregressive generation. The other study investigates a broader range of architectures, including decoder-only models (like GPT-3.5-Turbo, Claude-1.3, Llama-2) and encoder-decoder models (like Flan-T5-XXL, Flan-UL2).

query.content: What are the primary challenges identified by each study when dealing with long text or long input contexts in language models?

ground_truth.content: One study identifies the 'collapse problem' of pre-trained masked language models for long text generation, where they generate uninformative content with high-frequency and repeated tokens. The other study identifies that language model performance degrades significantly when relevant information is in the middle of long contexts, exhibiting a U-shaped performance curve (primacy and recency bias).

query.content: How do the two studies differ in their focus on inference efficiency?

ground_truth.content: One study explicitly focuses on improving and measuring inference efficiency for long text generation, reporting speeds of 133 to 1753 tokens/second and speedups of 2.9x to 13.3x compared to autoregressive models. The other study, while evaluating large language models, primarily focuses on how effectively models use long contexts rather than generation speed, though it mentions the cost of evaluating large models.

query.content: What types of LLMs are the focus of investigation in these two works?

ground_truth.content: One work conducts experiments using specific LLMs like Facebook OPT-6.7b and LLAMA2-7b to test its truthfulness detection method. The other work performs a conceptual analysis on general-purpose LLMs, including models like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, GPT-4, and Llama, to discuss the impossibility of fairness.

query.content: What are the reported accuracy scores for the QNLI task?

ground_truth.content: TinyBERT<sub>6</sub> achieved 90.4% accuracy on QNLI, and TinyBERT<sub>4</sub> achieved 87.7%. The BERT<sub>BASE</sub> teacher model achieved 90.9%. The Multi-task model from the GLUE benchmark paper achieved 81.7% accuracy on QNLI.

query.content: What are the main challenges concerning LLMs that these two works investigate?

ground_truth.content: One work investigates the challenge of LLMs generating inaccurate information and proposes a method to detect when an LLM 'knows' it's lying. The other work investigates the inherent intractability of achieving rigorous fairness in general-purpose LLMs.

query.content: How do the proposed methods compare in terms of their performance improvements over existing baselines?

ground_truth.content:
QST demonstrates significant efficiency gains, reducing memory footprint by up to 2.3x and speeding up finetuning by up to 3x compared to state-of-the-art methods like QLoRA. For larger models like OPT-6.7B, QST reduces memory footprint by 2.3x and trainable parameters by 5.5x with only a 1.3% accuracy drop. It also improves MMLU accuracy by 0.1% on average (up to 2.1% for LLaMA-2-13B) and chatbot performance by 0.46 points over QLoRA.

HYBGRAG, on the other hand, shows substantial accuracy improvements in retrieval, achieving an average relative improvement in Hit@1 of 51% (47% on STARK-MAG and 55% on STARK-PRIME) over its baselines on the STARK benchmark. It also significantly outperforms all baselines in end-to-end RAG on the CRAG benchmark, indicating its effectiveness in handling hybrid questions that combine textual and relational information.

query.content: How do the models compare in terms of accuracy on the SST-2 sentiment classification task?

ground_truth.content: TinyBERT<sub>6</sub> achieved 93.1% accuracy on SST-2, while TinyBERT<sub>4</sub> achieved 92.6%. The BERT<sub>BASE</sub> teacher model achieved 93.4%. The Multi-task model from the GLUE benchmark paper achieved 91.6% accuracy on SST-2.

query.content: What is the highest average GLUE score achieved by the models discussed?

ground_truth.content: The BERT<sub>BASE</sub> teacher model achieved an average GLUE score of 79.5. TinyBERT<sub>6</sub> achieved 79.4, performing on-par with its teacher. In contrast, the Multi-task model, one of the top baselines in the GLUE benchmark paper, achieved an average score of 69.0.
